cue: You see a wide band of ground. Out-of-focus things smear sideways.

DEUTAN.note: Vienot, Brettel and Mollon 1999, entered from memory

rows: White-tailed deer have two kinds of colour-sensing cells, where people have three. Reds and oranges look yellow or grey to them.
A deer takes in about 310 degrees around itself, almost a full circle. A phone camera sees less than a quarter of that, so this view bends the picture at its edges to suggest it.

Grazing animals have pupils shaped like horizontal bars. The shape widens their view along the ground and cuts glare from the sky. It also smears out-of-focus things sideways, and this view does the same.
These parts of the view are guesses. This view treats things lower in the picture as closer.

As the light falls, the colours drift toward what the rods take in, which peak near 497 nm. The peak is measured; where the change happens is the app's guess.

A deer sees in dim light partly by pooling light over time. With &draw=exposure, in the dark the picture pools the last few seconds, so still things settle and moving things leave ghosts. The pooling time is the app's.

windowS.note: seconds of pooling in the dark; the pooling time is the app's (atlas 7)

mix.note: how much of the pooled picture is shown, rising as the light falls
